title: Cast vs calendered vinyl
meta_title: Cast vs Calendered Vinyl for Vehicles | Broadland Digital
meta_description: Cast or calendered vinyl for your vehicle? Compare how each film is made, how it copes with curves, shrinkage, durability and cost, and when each makes sense.
html:
Compare your options

Cast vs calendered vinyl

Both are PVC films, but they are made differently and behave differently on a vehicle. Compare conformability, shrinkage, durability and cost to see which belongs on flat lettering and which on curves and recesses.

DISCUSS YOUR VEHICLE GRAPHICS ↗

In this comparison

The difference starts in manufacture.Compare at a glanceCast vinyl: made for curves and recesses.Calendered vinyl: dependable on flat panels.Printed graphics need a matching laminate.Adhesive is a separate decision.Three examples of how the job decides the film.What to ask for in a quote.What to send usQuestions & answersSources & further readingExplore the services

The difference starts in manufacture.

Most vehicle graphics films are PVC, but they are not all made the same way, and the method affects how the film behaves on a van. Cast vinyl starts as a liquid mixture that is spread thinly onto a carrier sheet and cured. Because it is formed without being stretched, it has little built-in tension. Calendered vinyl starts as a thicker mass that is pressed and rolled out between heated rollers to the required thickness. That process builds in some tension, and the film can try to return towards its original shape over time.

Neither is simply good or bad. They are designed for different jobs, at different price points. The useful question is which film suits the surface, the design and the length of time you need the graphics to last. A quote that only says “vinyl” leaves that question unanswered.

Compare at a glance.

On a smaller screen, scroll across to compare all options.

Cast vs calendered vinyl at a glance
FactorCast vinylCalendered vinyl
How it is madeLiquid spread thinly and curedPressed and rolled out between rollers
Typical thicknessGenerally thinnerGenerally thicker
Curves and recessesConforms and tends to stay putBest kept to flat or gentle curves
ShrinkageGenerally lowCan shrink back as tension relaxes
DurabilityTypically longer manufacturer ratingsShorter to medium term, product dependent
CostHigherLower
Typical vehicle useWraps, colour change, complex panelsCut lettering and flat graphics
Laminate (printed work)Use a matching cast laminateUse a compatible laminate
RemovalDepends on the adhesive and ageDepends on the adhesive and age

Cast vinyl: made for curves and recesses.

Cast films are generally thinner and more conformable. When warmed and worked into a recess, around a curve or over a rivet, they tend to stay where they are put rather than pulling back. That is why cast films are the usual choice for full and part wraps, colour-change wraps and printed graphics that cross pressings and complex panels.

Cast films are also generally more dimensionally stable over their life, with less shrinkage, and they typically carry longer manufacturer durability ratings. The trade-off is cost. Cast film costs more to make, and that is reflected in the price of a wrap. The colour-change wrap on the pickup pictured at the top of this page is the kind of job where a conformable film matters.

Calendered vinyl: dependable on flat panels.

Calendered films are typically thicker and stiffer. On a flat or gently curved surface, such as the side of a panel van, that is not a disadvantage, and a good calendered film can be a sensible choice for cut lettering and simpler graphics. It is easier to handle for some applications and costs less than cast.

Calendered films divide broadly into two groups. Polymeric calendered films are made with additives that help them stay stable for longer and are often used for medium-term vehicle and sign work. Monomeric calendered films are generally intended for shorter-term and flat applications. Pushing a calendered film into deep recesses or around tight curves invites lifting and shrinkage as its built-in tension tries to pull it back.

Printed graphics need a matching laminate.

When graphics are printed, a clear overlaminate usually goes on top to protect the ink from scuffs, washing and weathering. The laminate needs to be compatible with the base film. Put a calendered laminate over a cast wrap film and the two may behave differently on curves, with the laminate pulling back or lifting. Manufacturers typically pair specific laminates with specific print films.

Solid-colour cut vinyl does not normally need a laminate because the colour runs through the film. Our printers are 8-colour, 1440dpi machines producing prints roughly 1.5m wide by 50m long, and we can also cut from our in-house stock of pre-coloured vinyl. Which route is best depends on the design and the surface.

Adhesive is a separate decision.

Cast and calendered describe how the face film is made. The adhesive on the back is a separate choice. Some films use permanent adhesives and others are designed to be removable within a stated period. Many wrap films have air-release channels in the adhesive, which help push out air during fitting. These features exist on both cast and calendered products, so check the specific film rather than assuming.

If you know the graphics will need to come off at a particular point, such as the end of a lease, mention it at the start. The film and adhesive can be chosen with removal in mind. See graphics on leased vans for planning around a return date.

Three examples of how the job decides the film.

Illustrative example: a carpenter wants a company name and phone number on the flat sides and rear doors of a white panel van. The surfaces are flat, the lettering is solid colour and a good calendered or cast cut vinyl could both do the job. The decision comes down to expected life and budget.

Illustrative example: an owner wants a full colour-change wrap on a pickup with deep wheel arches and pressed panels. The film has to stretch into recesses and stay there. A cast wrap film is the appropriate starting point.

Illustrative example: a printed design runs across the side of a van with ribbed panels and rivets. Even if most of the side is flat, the design crosses features that need a conformable film. A cast print film with a matching cast laminate avoids a weak point where the film is stretched.

What to ask for in a quote.

Ask any supplier to name the manufacturer and product for both the film and the laminate, and to say whether each is cast or calendered. We use films from 3M and Metamark. Ask what durability the manufacturer quotes for that product, remembering that ratings apply to stated conditions and are not the same as a warranty on finished graphics.

Our van graphics will last up to 7 years if looked after correctly. Our guide to how long van wraps last covers the other factors, including where the van is parked and how it is washed.

Your project checklist.

  • Make, model and year of the vehicle.
  • Photographs showing the panels, curves, rivets and recesses involved.
  • Whether you want cut lettering, printed graphics or a colour-change wrap.
  • How long you expect to keep the graphics on the vehicle.
  • Whether the vehicle is owned, leased or financed.
  • Any quotes you are comparing, so the film specifications can be checked.

TALK THROUGH YOUR PROJECT ↗

Your questions. Answered.

Is cast vinyl always better?

Not always. Cast is the better choice for curves, recesses and full wraps. For flat lettering, a good calendered film can be a sensible, lower-cost option.

Can calendered vinyl be used for a full wrap?

It is not the usual choice. A full wrap stretches film into recesses and around curves, where calendered films are more likely to lift or shrink back. Cast wrap films are designed for this.

What is polymeric vinyl?

A calendered film made with additives that help it stay stable for longer. It sits between monomeric calendered and cast films in typical use and cost.

How can I tell which vinyl a quote includes?

Ask the supplier to name the manufacturer and product for the film and the laminate. A product name lets you check what it is designed for.

Do you use cast or calendered vinyl?

We use films from 3M and Metamark and choose the film to suit the job. Your quote can confirm the product for your vehicle.

title: Chapter 8 chevrons explained
meta_description: What Chapter 8 rear chevrons are, what to check with your client and the current guidance, and how chevron kits are cut, posted or fitted to your vehicles.
html:
Vehicle graphics guides & advice

Chapter 8 chevrons explained

If your vehicles stop or work on the highway, a client may ask for Chapter 8 chevrons on the rear. Here is what the term means, what to check before you order, and how kits are made and fitted.

DISCUSS YOUR VEHICLE GRAPHICS ↗

What people mean by Chapter 8.

Chapter 8 refers to a chapter of the Traffic Signs Manual, published by the Department for Transport, that deals with traffic safety measures for road works and temporary situations. Among other things, it gives guidance on making vehicles that work on or beside the road more visible to approaching traffic. In everyday use, “Chapter 8 chevrons” means the rear-facing pattern of alternating red and fluorescent yellow retroreflective stripes seen on the back of many highways, utility and works vehicles.

This page is a practical introduction, not a statement of what the guidance requires for your vehicles. The guidance is revised from time to time, and whether it applies depends on the work you do and where you do it. Always check the current version of the guidance and your client’s requirements before ordering.

Who usually asks for chevrons.

Rear chevrons are commonly seen on vehicles that stop, park or work on the highway: road maintenance and highways contractors, utility companies, local authority fleets, traffic management firms and some recovery and survey operators. Smaller trades may come across the requirement when they take on work for a highways client or a larger contractor.

Often the requirement arrives through a contract, a framework or a client’s own vehicle standard rather than from the guidance alone. Those documents can be more specific than the general guidance, setting out the material grade, the area to be covered or extra markings. If you have been asked to fit chevrons, ask the person who asked for a copy of the written requirement. Our page on highways and utilities vehicle graphics covers fleet identification and high-visibility livery for these operators.

Check the guidance and your client’s specification.

Do not rely on copying the van parked next to yours. Another operator’s vehicle may have been fitted to an older version of the guidance, a different client standard or no standard at all. Before you order, find out which version of the guidance applies, whether your client specifies a particular material or class of reflective film, and what coverage of the rear is expected.

Bring that information to us with your enquiry. We can make chevrons to suit the vehicle, but it is your responsibility, and that of your client, to confirm what is required for the work. If the specification is unclear, ask the client to confirm it in writing before the kit is cut. That avoids paying twice for a kit that does not meet the brief.

Pre-cut kits for mainstream vehicles.

We offer Chapter 8 reflective kits for the majority of mainstream vehicles. We keep up-to-date databases of vehicle outlines, so a kit can be cut to the shape of your rear doors, working around handles, hinges, windows, lights and the number plate area. A pre-cut kit saves time on fitting and gives a consistent result across several vehicles of the same model.

To match a kit to your vehicle, we need the make, model, year, roof height and rear door configuration. Twin rear doors, a tailgate, a tipper body and a box body all need different layouts. A photograph of the rear of the vehicle is the quickest way to confirm we are working from the right outline.

Bespoke chevrons for unusual bodies.

Not every vehicle is in a database. Conversions, flatbeds, tippers, box bodies, trailers and specialist equipment often need bespoke chevrons. We produce bespoke cut reflectives using our in-house drag-knife and laser cutters, which allows accurate shapes in reflective materials.

For a bespoke job, send clear photographs of the rear of the vehicle taken square-on, plus measurements of each flat area you want covered. Mark anything that must stay clear, such as lights, reflectors, the number plate, camera lenses, handles and hinges. If the body has a tail lift or a drop-down tailgate, tell us, because the chevrons need to work with the vehicle in its normal driving position.

Fitting: at our workshop or by you.

If you are close to Norwich, you can bring the vehicle to our workshop for fitting. If you are further away, you can ask for a quote for on-site fitting, or we can post a kit for you to fit yourself in your own yard.

If you fit a kit yourself, work on a clean, dry, grease-free surface in mild conditions. Fit one panel at a time, line each section up against a fixed reference such as the door edge, and press the film down firmly from the centre outwards. Do not cover lights, reflectors, the number plate or the rear windows. Cut at door shuts rather than bridging them, so doors open without lifting the film.

Plan chevrons alongside your livery.

Chevrons usually take up most of the rear of a van, which is often where the company name, phone number and web address would go. Plan both together. Contact details can move to the side panels or sit on a band above or below the chevrons if the guidance and your client allow. Our van graphics team can lay out the livery and the chevrons as one design.

Side markings and other conspicuity features are a separate question from rear chevrons. If you are unsure what your vehicles need on the sides, check the guidance and your client’s standard rather than assuming the rear kit covers everything. Chevrons do not replace beacons, lighting or any other equipment your work requires.

Keep reflectives clean and intact.

Reflective film only works when light can reach it. Road dirt, salt and mud on the rear doors reduce how well chevrons show up in headlights, so include the rear of the vehicle in regular washing. Avoid abrasive pads and harsh solvents, which can damage the reflective surface.

Check chevrons as part of routine vehicle checks. Look for damaged, faded or missing sections, especially around door handles and lower edges where loading and reversing take their toll. Keep a note of the vehicle details and kit reference so a replacement panel can be ordered quickly when needed.

Your project checklist.

  • Make, model, year, roof height and rear door configuration of each vehicle.
  • A square-on photograph of the rear of each vehicle type.
  • Your client’s written specification, if you have one.
  • Measurements and photos for any bespoke body, trailer or conversion.
  • Whether you want workshop fitting, a quote for on-site fitting or a posted kit.
  • How many vehicles, and whether livery should be designed at the same time.

TALK THROUGH YOUR PROJECT ↗

Your questions. Answered.

Are Chapter 8 chevrons a legal requirement for my van?

That depends on the work you do and where you do it. We cannot advise on whether they are required for your work. Check the current guidance and your client’s requirements, and ask your client to confirm the specification in writing.

Can you post a chevron kit for me to fit myself?

Yes. If you are not local, we can supply kits by post for self-installation. Fit them on a clean, dry surface and keep lights, the number plate and windows clear.

My vehicle is not a standard van. Can you still make chevrons?

Yes. We produce bespoke cut reflectives with our drag-knife and laser cutters. Send square-on photographs and measurements of the areas to be covered.

Can my company logo go on the rear doors as well?

Plan the rear layout with the chevrons first. Contact details often move to the sides. Check the guidance and your client’s standard before placing anything else on the chevron area.

Do chevrons replace beacons or lights?

No. Rear chevrons are one part of making a vehicle conspicuous. Lighting, beacons and other equipment are separate requirements to check with your client and the guidance.

Fleet graphics.

Every vehicle. One identity.

A single van can carry a design that was worked out on the day. A fleet cannot. Once you have five, twenty or fifty vehicles on the road, people start to recognise the livery before they read it, and any vehicle that looks slightly different weakens that recognition. The logo drifts in size, the blue is a shade off, the phone number moves from the door to the rear panel. Customers notice, even if they could not say why.

Fleet graphics are therefore as much about planning as design. The livery has to work on every vehicle type you run: a small car-derived van, a long-wheelbase high-roof van, a pickup, a minibus or a car transporter. Each has different panel shapes, door positions and windows. A good fleet design is built so it can be adapted to each body while still looking like the same company.

It also has to last beyond the first rollout. Vehicles are replaced, added and occasionally damaged. Your livery needs to be easy to reproduce accurately whenever that happens, without starting the design process again.

Write the rules once.

Fleet brand standard

Same positions. Same colours. Every model.

We agree a simple standard for your fleet: where the logo sits relative to the wheel arch or door line, the minimum height of the phone number, which vinyl colours match your brand, and how the rear doors are laid out. That standard is then applied to each vehicle type in turn.

SidesLogo and core message, positioned from fixed reference points
RearContact details and fleet or vehicle number
Front & bonnetName, plus a vehicle number if your depot uses one

We keep up-to-date databases of vehicle outlines, so a mock-up can be prepared for each model in your fleet before production.

Choose a level for the whole fleet.

Fleets often run more than one level: full livery on customer-facing vans and simpler lettering on pool cars or support vehicles. Our supply-and-fit packages (per vehicle, fitted within a 30-mile radius of Norwich) are a useful starting point. All prices are “from” and + VAT, and a quote for your fleet confirms the figures.

Basic, from £149 + VAT ↗

Single-colour cut vinyl name on the bonnet, sides and rear, with phone and web details. Ideal for support vehicles and pool vans.

Standard, from £210 + VAT ↗

Adds a second colour or panel infill, social media details and a cut or printed logo, subject to complexity and hi-res files.

Pro & full livery, from £455 + VAT ↗

Pro adds design options (up to three ideas) and large rear-quarter and rear graphics. Bespoke fleet livery is quoted per design.

Part & full wraps ↗

Printed coverage or a colour change, from cars to a 56-seater coach. Quoted for each vehicle type in the fleet.

Rollouts, replacements and repairs.

Rolling out. Few businesses can take every vehicle off the road at once. We plan the fitting schedule with you, typically in batches, around the vehicles you can spare. Courtesy vehicles are also available while a vehicle is off the road.

New and replacement vehicles. When a new van joins the fleet, we work from the approved artwork and the agreed standard, so it matches the vehicles already in service. If the new van is a different model, we adapt the layout and send you a proof first.

Damage. Vehicle graphics are semi-permanent. If a panel is repaired after a scrape, the graphics on that panel can usually be replaced without redoing the whole vehicle.

Leaving the fleet. Graphics can be removed before a vehicle is sold or returned. If your fleet is leased, check the return conditions; our guide to graphics on leased vans explains what to ask.

What to send us.

For a fleet quote, a short spreadsheet is more useful than a long email. Include:

  • A list of vehicles: make, model, year, wheelbase and roof height for each.
  • Which vehicles get which level of graphics, if they differ.
  • Your brand guidelines, logo files (vector) and any brand colour references.
  • Photographs of a typical vehicle of each type, or of existing livery you want to match.
  • Fleet or vehicle numbering rules, if you use them.
  • Where vehicles are based and how many can be off the road at one time.

SEND YOUR FLEET LIST ↗

A clear process. From start to finish.

01

Audit the fleet.

We review your vehicle list and brand files, and note any existing livery that needs removing or matching.

02

Design the standard.

Our design department adapts the livery to each vehicle type and sends mock-ups for approval, or works with your own design team.

03

Produce in-house.

Printing and cutting happen at our Norwich workshop on large-format printers and plotter cutters, using 3M and Metamark materials.

04

We fit to the agreed schedule and keep the approved artwork on file for the next vehicle that joins the fleet.

Your questions. Answered.

Can you match the graphics on our existing vehicles?

Usually, yes. Send photographs and the original artwork if you have it. We can match vinyl colours from our in-house stock or print to your brand colours, and we will show you a proof before production.

Our fleet includes several different vehicle models. Will the livery look the same?

The design is adapted to each body shape, but the logo, colours, wording and positioning rules stay consistent. We prepare a mock-up for each model using our database of vehicle outlines.

Some of our vehicles are based outside Norfolk. Can you still help?

Vehicles can be brought to our Norwich workshop. For vehicles further afield, kits can be posted for self-installation where suitable, or ask us to quote for on-site fitting.

How long will fleet graphics last?

Fleet vehicles fitted with our 3M and Metamark graphics can expect up to 7 years of life when looked after correctly. Vehicles on long daily routes or washed frequently by brush machines may need closer attention.

Is there a price per vehicle for the whole fleet?

Our packages start from £149, £210 and £455 + VAT per vehicle. A fleet quote reflects the number and types of vehicle, the design and the fitting schedule, so ask us to price your list.

Food trucks · catering trailers · coffee vans

Food van wraps.

At an event or a lay-by, your van is the shopfront. Graphics that tell a hungry queue what you sell, from the far side of the field.

DISCUSS YOUR VAN ↗CALL 01603 407786

Norwich workshop · NR6 6AQ · Monday–Friday, 8:30am–5pm

Vehicle graphics / Sectors / Food van wraps
Your shopfrontWhat goes whereOptions & pricesCleaning & hygieneWhat to send usProcessFAQsDiscuss your van ↗

A shopfront on wheels.

A food truck, catering trailer or coffee van does two very different jobs. On the road it is an advert, seen briefly by passing traffic. Once parked at a market, festival or wedding, it becomes the shop: people walk across a field, scan a row of traders and decide where to queue in a few seconds. The graphics have to work in both situations.

From a distance, the most useful thing your van can say is what you sell. A name alone rarely does that. “Wood-fired pizza”, “Specialty coffee” or “Smash burgers” in large, simple lettering, ideally on the serving side and above the hatch, tells a customer whether to walk over. Strong colour and a recognisable logo help returning customers find you again at the next event.

Up close, the questions change. People want to know what is on the menu, whether you take cards and where you will be next week. That information changes often, so it usually suits removable boards or a printed panel that can be swapped, rather than lettering built into a full wrap.

What goes where.

Layout

Serving side first.

Start with the side customers queue at. Measure the hatch, awning and any fold-down counter, and keep important lettering clear of them when they are open. Hinges, vents and gas lockers interrupt panels too, so mark them on your photographs.

Above the hatchWhat you sell, in a few words
Road side & rearName, logo, social handles and booking contact
Lower panelsPhone number and web address for event bookings

The rear and the road side are seen while you travel and when you pitch with your back to a path. These are good places for “available for private hire” and your booking details, since event organisers often notice a van and get in touch later.

From lettering to a full colour change.

Some traders want a bold, fully printed van; others prefer a clean base colour with a few well-placed graphics. Our published supply-and-fit packages apply to vans fitted within a 30-mile radius of our Norwich workshop. Prices are “from” and + VAT, and your quote confirms the figure. Trailers and custom bodies are quoted individually.

Lettering packages, from £149 + VAT ↗

Basic cut-vinyl name and contact details from £149 + VAT; Standard adds a logo, a second colour and social media from £210 + VAT.

Pro graphics, from £455 + VAT ↗

Design options beyond the standard layout (up to three ideas) with a large logo or graphic on the rear quarters and rear.

Printed part & full wraps ↗

Photography, illustration or pattern across the whole body, printed in-house on 8-colour, 1440dpi printers. Quoted per vehicle.

Liquid wrapping ↗

A spray-applied colour change, as an alternative way to change the base colour of the vehicle. Ask whether it suits your van.

Cleaning, grease and hygiene.

Food vans are washed more often than most commercial vehicles, and the area around the serving hatch can pick up splashes, grease and steam. Vinyl graphics cope well with regular gentle cleaning, but a few habits help them last. Typically: wash by hand with a mild detergent, avoid harsh solvents and degreasers on printed areas, and keep a pressure washer away from the edges of the graphics.

Think about placement around heat and moisture. Extractor outlets, flues and the area directly above a fryer or coffee machine vent are not good places for detailed graphics, and edges near the hatch seal take the most wear. We can plan the design so these zones carry plain colour, which is easier to keep clean and simpler to replace.

Graphics are an exterior finish. Your food hygiene obligations, and anything your local authority’s environmental health team or an event organiser asks for, apply to the van as a whole. Check their requirements, and those of your gas and electrical installers, before you finalise a design that covers vents or access panels.

What to send us.

Food vans vary more than almost any other vehicle, from converted classics to purpose-built trailers. Help us quote accurately with:

  • The base vehicle or trailer make, model and year, plus any conversion details.
  • Photographs of every side with the hatch and awning both open and closed.
  • Rough measurements of the hatch, counter, vents and lockers.
  • Your logo files, brand colours and the one line that says what you sell.
  • Social handles, booking email and phone number for private hire.
  • Your first event date, so we can discuss a realistic production plan.

SEND YOUR VAN DETAILS ↗

A clear process. From start to finish.

01

Share your idea.

Send photographs, your menu concept and any branding. If you are just starting out, our design department can develop the look with you.

02

See it on your van.

We prepare a mock-up on your vehicle or trailer, including the hatch and awning, and refine it until you approve the proof.

03

Print and cut.

Full-colour panels are printed in-house; lettering is cut from our stock of coloured vinyl. We use 3M and Metamark materials.

04

Fit before the season.

We fit at our Norwich workshop on an agreed date. Booking ahead of your first event leaves room for any changes.

Your questions. Answered.

Should I put my menu and prices on the wrap?

Yes. Trailers are among the vehicles we produce graphics for. Send photographs and measurements of each side, including the hatch and drawbar area, and we will quote for your trailer.

Hand wash with a mild detergent and soft cloth, avoid harsh solvents on printed areas and keep pressure washers back from the edges. We will give you aftercare advice for your specific materials when you collect.

Our van graphics use 3M and Metamark materials and will last up to 7 years if looked after correctly. Areas near heat vents and the hatch seal see the most wear, which is why we plan the design around them.

Seen. Then identified.

Vehicles used for highway maintenance, street works, utilities, grounds and waste services spend much of their working day stopped where other traffic does not expect them: in a live lane, on a verge, at a junction or reversing into a site. Their graphics have two jobs, in a fixed order. First, make the vehicle conspicuous to approaching drivers, especially from behind and in poor light. Second, make it clear who the vehicle belongs to and which vehicle it is.

The first job is mainly about reflective materials and rear markings, and it is often governed by guidance and by the requirements of the client you are working for. The second is about livery and fleet identification: company or council name, depot, vehicle number and a contact number the public can use. Both need to be planned together, so branding does not crowd out the markings that matter most for safety.

We produce Chapter 8 reflective kits for most mainstream vehicles, and can cut bespoke reflectives for unusual bodies using our in-house drag-knife and laser cutters.

Layout

The rear of a works vehicle is where conspicuity markings matter most, so it is usually planned first. Rear doors, tailgates, tail lifts and tipper bodies all affect how a chevron kit is cut and where it can go. Lights, number plates, handles and hinges have to stay clear.

Chapter 8, in general terms.

“Chapter 8” refers to the part of the Traffic Signs Manual that deals with traffic safety measures for road works and temporary situations. Among other things, it covers how vehicles working on the highway should be made conspicuous. In practice, many people use “Chapter 8” as shorthand for the rear-facing chevron markings, typically in alternating red and fluorescent yellow retroreflective material, seen on works vehicles.

Whether a particular vehicle needs these markings, and the exact specification, depends on the work it does, the roads it works on and the current guidance. Highway authorities, utility companies and principal contractors also set their own vehicle requirements in contracts and site rules, which may go further than the minimum. Before ordering, check the current guidance and ask your client for their written vehicle specification. Send it with your enquiry and we will produce the kit to suit.

Vehicle graphics guides & advice

How long do van wraps last?

Vinyl on a van can look good for years, but the figure depends on the film, the panels it sits on, how the van is used and how it is cleaned. Here is what affects the life of a wrap and how to get the most from it.

DISCUSS YOUR VEHICLE GRAPHICS ↗
Vehicle graphics ↗ / Guides & advice ↗ / How long do van wraps last?
Guides & advice ↗Trades & sectors ↗Locations ↗

In this guide

The short answer, and why it comes with conditions.The film and laminate set the ceiling.Where on the van the vinyl sits.How the van is used and parked.Preparation and fitting matter as much as the film.Aftercare that helps vinyl last.Signs that graphics are near the end of their life.Refresh, repair or replace?What to send usQuestions & answersSources & further readingExplore the services

The short answer, and why it comes with conditions.

Our van graphics, made with 3M and Metamark films, will last up to 7 years if looked after correctly. That is a sensible planning figure, but it is not a promise that every panel on every van will look identical for seven years. The film, the way it was fitted, the shape of the panel it sits on and the life the van leads all have a say.

Manufacturers publish durability figures for their films, and those figures are tied to specific products and test conditions. A durability rating for a film is not the same as a warranty on your finished vehicle graphics. When you compare quotes, ask which product is specified and what applies to the completed job. That conversation is more useful than comparing headline numbers of years.

The film and laminate set the ceiling.

Vinyl films are made in different ways for different jobs. Cast films are generally thinner and more stable, and they cope better with curves, recesses and rivets. Calendered films are typically thicker and better suited to flatter surfaces and shorter-term work. Our cast vs calendered vinyl comparison explains the difference in more detail.

Printed graphics usually have a clear laminate over the print. The laminate protects the ink from abrasion and weathering, and it needs to be compatible with the base film. A good print film with a poorly matched laminate, or no laminate at all, will not reach the life of a properly specified system. Cut vinyl in a solid colour does not need a laminate because the colour runs through the film.

Where on the van the vinyl sits.

Not every part of a van wears at the same rate. Horizontal surfaces such as the bonnet and roof face the sun more directly than the vertical sides, so they tend to show fading and weathering first. If you are planning a long-life design, keep in mind that the bonnet may need attention before the side panels.

Vinyl is also under more stress where it has been stretched into a recess, wrapped around a sharp edge or pushed over a rivet. Those are the places where lifting tends to start. A good design and fitting plan reduces stretch where possible, trims at door shuts rather than forcing film around them and avoids placing fine details across awkward pressings.

How the van is used and parked.

A van kept in a yard under cover leads a different life from one parked outside a house facing south. Strong sun is a major factor in how quickly colours fade and how quickly film becomes brittle. Coastal air, regular motorway miles, road salt, site mud and tree sap all add to the wear.

Working habits matter too. Ladders slid across a roof, tools leaned against side panels and loading at the rear doors all scuff vinyl. Roof bars and racks can trap grit against the film. You cannot change how your business uses the van, but you can tell us about it so the layout keeps important graphics away from the areas that take the most punishment.

Preparation and fitting matter as much as the film.

Vinyl only performs as well as its bond to the paint. Panels need to be clean and free of wax, polish and silicone before application. Paint condition matters: chips, corrosion and flaking lacquer will not improve under vinyl, and fresh or aftermarket paint can need time to cure. Tell us about any recent bodywork repairs before the fitting day.

Temperature and conditions affect how film behaves during application. Fitting in a workshop gives control over cleanliness, light and temperature, so ask where your graphics will be fitted when you book. If you fit a posted kit yourself, follow the instructions supplied and choose a dry, sheltered day.

Aftercare that helps vinyl last.

Wash the van regularly, ideally by hand, with a mild vehicle shampoo and plenty of clean water. Dirt left on the surface holds moisture and pollutants against the film. Rinse thoroughly and dry with a clean, soft cloth. Ask us how long to leave new graphics before the first wash, as the adhesive needs time to settle.

If you use a pressure washer, keep the nozzle well back from the surface and do not aim it directly at the edges of the vinyl, where a strong jet can lift the film. Avoid harsh solvents, abrasive pads and cutting compounds. Wipe off fuel spills, bird droppings and tree sap promptly. Matt, satin and textured films need products suited to their finish, so check before using any wax or polish.

Signs that graphics are near the end of their life.

Ageing vinyl tends to show itself gradually. Look for colours that have faded noticeably compared with the original, a chalky surface, fine cracking, edges that have started to lift, or a thin line of adhesive showing where the film has shrunk back. On printed graphics, wear often starts on the bonnet and roof.

Once the film becomes brittle, removal usually takes longer because it breaks into small pieces rather than peeling away. If you plan to replace the graphics anyway, doing it before they deteriorate badly can make removal more straightforward. Take photographs of any problem areas and send them to us with the vehicle details.

Refresh, repair or replace?

Vehicle graphics are semi-permanent, so you have options. A damaged section of a wrap can often be reprinted and replaced if the artwork and film details are on file. Lettering on a single panel can be renewed without touching the rest of the van. When a business changes its phone number or adds a service, an update can be quicker than a full redesign.

Keep a record of the approved artwork, the film and laminate used and the date the graphics were fitted. That makes repairs and repeat orders straightforward, and it helps if you add vans to a fleet later. If you are not sure whether to repair or replace, our team can look at photographs and talk through the options.

Your project checklist.

  • Make, model and year of the van, and when the current graphics were fitted.
  • Photographs of the whole van and close-ups of any wear or damage.
  • Whether the graphics are printed, cut vinyl or a colour-change wrap.
  • How the van is used and parked, including racks, ladders or coastal use.
  • How long you plan to keep the van.
  • Your artwork files, if you want sections reprinted or replaced.

TALK THROUGH YOUR PROJECT ↗

Your questions. Answered.

How long will my van graphics last?

Our van graphics will last up to 7 years if looked after correctly. Sun exposure, the panel shape, the film, the fitting and how the van is washed all affect the result.

Can I use a pressure washer on a wrapped van?

Yes, with care. Keep the nozzle well back and do not aim the jet at the edges of the vinyl. Hand washing with a mild shampoo is gentler.

Why does the bonnet fade first?

Horizontal surfaces face the sun more directly than the sides of the van, so they usually weather more quickly. This is normal, and a bonnet can be renewed on its own.

Does a manufacturer’s durability figure mean my wrap is guaranteed for that long?

No. A film’s rating applies to that product under stated conditions. Ask what applies to your finished graphics when you receive the quote.

Can one damaged panel be replaced?

Usually, yes. Keep the approved artwork and film details, and send photographs of the damage so we can advise on reprinting or replacing that section.

Vehicle graphics guides & advice

How much do van graphics cost?

The price of van graphics depends on how much of the van you cover, how the design is produced and who fits it. Here is what our published packages include, what moves a quote up or down and how to compare prices fairly.

Start with what the graphics need to do.

A van that only needs to show who you are and how to reach you is a very different job from a van designed to be noticed across a car park. Before asking for a price, decide what the graphics must achieve. The answer sets the coverage, and coverage is the biggest single influence on cost.

A price quoted without that context is hard to judge. Tell us the make, model, wheelbase and roof height of the van, the colour it is painted and roughly what you want on it. Side and rear photographs help even more, because they show the panels, handles, windows and pressings the design has to work around.

What our published supply-and-fit packages include.

For straightforward van lettering we publish three supply-and-fit packages, fitted within a 30-mile radius of our Norwich workshop. They are intended as a starting point for budgeting. The price for your particular van is confirmed by a quote once we know the vehicle and have seen your artwork.

Basic graphics, from £149 + VAT. Single-colour cut vinyl of your company name to the bonnet, both side panels and the rear, with your web address and phone number on the lower side panels and the bottom of the rear doors.

Standard graphics, from £210 + VAT. Everything in Basic, plus social media details, a second vinyl colour or a panel infill, and a cut or printed logo. The logo is subject to its complexity and to you having high-resolution files available.

Pro graphics, from £455 + VAT. Everything in Basic and Standard, plus design options over and above regular graphic placement (up to three ideas) and a large logo or graphic element on the rear quarters and rear.

These packages are built around lettering and logos applied to the van’s existing paint colour. They are not full printed wraps. A wrap involves far more material, printing and fitting time, varies widely between vehicles and is quoted individually. If you are weighing the two approaches, our van wrap vs part graphics comparison sets out the differences.

Supply only: fitting the graphics yourself.

If you are comfortable applying vinyl, or you are too far from Norwich for fitting to make sense, our online shop sells supply-only van graphics. Current shop prices start from £95 + VAT for Basic graphics on a small van, from £125 + VAT for Basic on a medium van, from £150 + VAT for Standard on a small van and from £225 + VAT for Standard on a medium van. There is also an online design builder on our van graphics page if you want to lay out your own design.

The saving is the fitting labour, and with it comes the responsibility for application. Vinyl needs a clean, dry, grease-free panel, a sensible temperature and patience with alignment. Be honest about the time and conditions you have before choosing self-fit purely on price.

What moves a quote up or down.

Van size and coverage. A long-wheelbase, high-roof van has more panel area than a small car-derived van, so the same layout needs more vinyl and more fitting time. Adding panels, such as the roof line, rear quarters or bonnet, increases both.

Cut or printed. Single-colour cut vinyl is the simplest route. Each extra colour is usually another layer to cut, weed and apply. Printed logos, gradients and photographs are produced on our 8-colour, 1440dpi printers and then cut to shape. We hold a large stock of coloured vinyl in-house, so a pre-coloured film is often the practical choice for solid lettering.

Panel shape. Ribbed panels, rivets, deep pressings and sliding-door channels take longer to work around and can affect which film is suitable. Our cast vs calendered vinyl guide explains why.

Old graphics. Removing existing vinyl adds time, and how long it takes is not always clear until the work starts. Older, sun-baked vinyl tends to come off in small pieces. Mention any existing graphics in your enquiry so they can be allowed for.

Extras. Chapter 8 rear chevrons, reflective materials, window graphics and matching graphics for a trailer all add to the job. Ask for them in the same quote so the layouts can be planned together.

Artwork is where hidden costs often sit.

The Standard package includes a cut or printed logo on the condition that you can supply high-resolution files. That condition matters. A logo saved from a social media profile or a website header is usually too small and too soft to scale up to the side of a van. It may need redrawing before it can be cut or printed cleanly, and that is design time.

Ask whoever designed your logo for the original vector file, often supplied as AI, EPS, SVG or a vector PDF. If that is not available, our in-house design department can recreate it or design from scratch, and we will work with your own design team if you have one. Settle wording and phone numbers before approving the proof.

Fitting, location and time off the road.

Our supply-and-fit packages cover a 30-mile radius of the Norwich workshop. If you are further out, you can bring the van to us, choose a posted self-install kit where the design is suitable, or ask for a quote for on-site fitting. Tell us your postcode at the start so the quote reflects the right option.

Time off the road is a real cost for a business that depends on its van. We have courtesy vehicles available while your van is with us, which is worth asking about when you book. Tell us about any recent paint repairs, as fresh paint can need time to cure before vinyl goes on.

How to compare van graphics quotes fairly.

When you have more than one quote, line them up against the same specification. Check which panels are covered, how many colours are included, whether the logo is cut or printed, which brand and type of vinyl is specified, whether fitting is included and where it happens, whether removal of old graphics is included, how many design revisions are allowed and whether the figure includes VAT. Our prices are always shown + VAT.

Differences between quotes usually sit in the material, the coverage or the fitting. We use 3M and Metamark films. Ask any supplier to name the product so you can compare like with like. Our blog post on comparing van graphics quotes and coverage goes into more detail.

Think about cost per year, not just the invoice.

Van graphics are semi-permanent. They can be updated, replaced or removed, and they will last up to 7 years if looked after correctly. Spread over the time you keep the van, a modest difference at the start becomes small. Our guide to graphics on leased vans covers that situation.

Illustrative example: a newly established electrician starts with Basic graphics on a white van, keeping the phone number on its own line. A year later the business adds a printed logo and a second colour without replacing the lettering already on the van. Another business might go straight to Pro so the rear carries a large logo from day one. The right budget follows the brief.

Your project checklist.

  • Make, model, year, wheelbase and roof height of the van.
  • Side, rear and front photographs, including any existing graphics.
  • Your logo as a vector or high-resolution file, and the exact wording.
  • Which package you are considering, or a sketch of what you want where.
  • Your postcode and whether you want fitting, a posted kit or to visit us.
  • Any date you are working towards and whether you need a courtesy vehicle.

TALK THROUGH YOUR PROJECT ↗

Your questions. Answered.

Do your van graphics prices include VAT?

No. All of our published prices are shown + VAT and are “from” prices. The figure for your van is confirmed by a quote once we know the vehicle and have seen the artwork.

Does the Pro package include a full wrap?

No. Pro covers lettering, logos and extra design options, including a large logo or graphic element on the rear quarters and rear. Full and part wraps are quoted individually.

Can you fit the graphics if I am more than 30 miles from Norwich?

The packages are fitted within a 30-mile radius. Further out, you can bring the van to our Norwich workshop, choose a posted self-install kit where suitable, or ask us to quote for on-site fitting.

I only have my logo as a JPEG. Is that a problem?

Not necessarily, but a small or low-resolution image may need redrawing before it can be cut or printed cleanly. Send what you have and we will tell you whether it can be used as supplied.

Can I get a price from photographs?

Yes, photographs with the make and model are enough for an initial price. The quote is confirmed once the final layout and artwork are agreed.

Vehicle graphics guides & advice

Graphics on leased vans: fitting and removal

Most leased and financed vans can carry vinyl graphics, but the van still has to go back in an acceptable condition. Here is what to check before you brand a van you do not own, and how to plan for removal at the end of the agreement.

DISCUSS YOUR VEHICLE GRAPHICS ↗
Vehicle graphics ↗ / Guides & advice ↗ / Graphics on leased vans: fitting and removal
Guides & advice ↗Trades & sectors ↗Locations ↗

In this guide

Read the agreement before the artwork.Why vinyl suits a vehicle you will hand back.Design with the hand-back in mind.What happens to the paint underneath.How removal is done.Plan the timing around the return date.Moving the branding to the next van.Include removal in the cost of branding.What to send usQuestions & answersSources & further readingExplore the services

Read the agreement before the artwork.

Many businesses run vans on contract hire, lease or finance, and most of them want those vans branded. Vinyl graphics are well suited to that, but the van has to go back, or be valued, in an acceptable condition. The first step is not design. It is reading what your agreement says about modifications, signwriting and the condition expected at the end.

Agreements differ. Some say nothing specific about graphics, some ask you to seek permission first, and some describe what must be removed before return. Under some finance agreements you may own the van at the end, while under contract hire it goes back to the provider. If anything is unclear, ask the leasing or finance company in writing and keep the reply. It is far easier to settle this before the van is branded than at hand-back.

Why vinyl suits a vehicle you will hand back.

Vinyl graphics are semi-permanent. Unlike painted signwriting, they sit on top of the paint and can be replaced or removed when the van changes hands. That makes them a practical way to brand a vehicle you do not own outright, provided the graphics, the paint and the removal are planned sensibly.

Removable does not mean effortless. How easily graphics come off depends on the film and its adhesive, how long the graphics have been on the van, how much sun the van has seen and the condition of the paint underneath. Tell us at the quoting stage that the van is leased and roughly how long the agreement runs. That helps us suggest a film and layout that suit the period you will keep it.

Design with the hand-back in mind.

Coverage is the biggest factor in how long removal takes. Cut lettering and a logo on the side and rear panels are quicker to remove than a full wrap. If a lease runs for a few years, a design built around the van’s own paint colour may be the better investment than covering every panel. Our van wrap vs part graphics comparison sets out the trade-offs.

Keep graphics on the van’s original, manufacturer-applied paint where possible. Aftermarket repairs and resprayed panels are more likely to have a weaker bond between paint and primer, which raises the risk of paint lifting when vinyl is removed later. Photograph every panel before fitting and keep the images with your lease paperwork. That record shows the condition of the van when it was branded.

What happens to the paint underneath.

While vinyl is on the van, the paint beneath it is shaded from the sun. The surrounding paint is exposed and can weather slightly over the years. On some vehicles, especially older ones or those in strong colours, that difference can leave a faint outline of the graphics after removal, sometimes called ghosting. It often reduces with cleaning and polishing, but it is not always fully avoidable.

Adhesive residue is the other common issue. Some adhesive can stay behind when old vinyl is peeled, particularly where the film has aged. It needs to be removed with a product suitable for automotive paint, followed by a wash. Scraping with a blade or using harsh solvents risks damaging the paint and creating the kind of mark a return inspection will notice.

How removal is done.

Removal usually involves gently warming the vinyl to soften the adhesive, then peeling it back at a low angle so it comes away slowly. Newer graphics often come off in large pieces. Older, sun-baked film tends to break into small fragments and takes much longer. After the vinyl is off, any adhesive residue is cleaned away and the panels are washed and inspected.

A pressure washer is not a removal tool. Aiming a jet at the edge of the vinyl can lift paint as well as film, and leaves the job half done. If you plan to remove the graphics yourself, use plastic tools, take your time and stop if paint starts to come away with the vinyl. If you would rather we did it, tell us the vehicle, the age of the graphics and when the van is due back, and we can discuss it.

Plan the timing around the return date.

Do not leave removal to the last day. Book it well before the van is due back so there is time to deal with residue, wash the van and look at it in daylight. If the removal reveals a mark or outline, you then have time to decide how to handle it before the inspection, rather than finding out on the day.

Check what the leasing company expects at return. Many refer to fair wear and tear guidance, and some will accept a van with graphics still applied while others will not. Ask in advance and plan accordingly. Your agreement and your provider’s guidance are the authority here, not general advice.

Moving the branding to the next van.

A lease ending usually means a new van arriving. Keep the approved artwork, the colours and the vinyl specification from the first van so the replacement can be branded consistently. The layout may need adjusting if the new van is a different model, because door positions, pressings and windows vary, but the design itself carries over.

We have courtesy vehicles available while a van is off the road, which can help if removal from the old van and fitting on the new one need to happen close together. If you run several vehicles, our page on fleet graphics covers rollouts and replacements across a fleet.

Include removal in the cost of branding.

When you budget for graphics on a leased van, think about the whole period: design, supply and fitting at the start, any updates along the way, and removal at the end. Our published supply-and-fit packages for van graphics start from £149 + VAT and are confirmed by quote. The effort involved in removal depends on the coverage and condition of the graphics, so raise it when you ask for your quote.

Illustrative example: a building firm leases three vans for a fixed term. It chooses cut vinyl lettering with a printed logo on manufacturer paint, photographs every van before fitting and books removal a few weeks before the return date. The work at the end is predictable, and the artwork moves straight on to the replacement vans.

Your project checklist.

  • The relevant section of your lease or finance agreement, or the provider’s reply.
  • Make, model, year and paint colour of the van, and the lease end date.
  • Photographs of every panel before the graphics are fitted.
  • Details of any bodywork repairs or resprayed panels.
  • For removal: the age of the graphics and recent photographs.
  • Your artwork files, if the branding is moving to a replacement van.

Your questions. Answered.

Can I put graphics on a leased van?

Often, yes, but check your agreement first. Some providers ask you to seek permission or set out what must be removed before return. Ask in writing if it is unclear.

Will removing vinyl damage the paint?

On sound manufacturer paint, careful removal usually leaves the paint intact. Resprayed panels, old brittle film and poor paint condition increase the risk. Photograph the van before fitting so you have a record.

What is ghosting?

A faint outline where graphics have been. The paint under the vinyl is shaded from sunlight while the rest of the van is not. It often reduces with cleaning and polishing but cannot always be removed completely.

How far ahead should I book removal?

Allow time before the return date to remove the vinyl, clean off residue and check the van in daylight. Leaving it to the final day leaves no time to deal with anything unexpected.

Can you put the same graphics on my next van?

Yes. Keep the approved artwork and the vinyl specification. The layout may need adjusting for a different model, and the new van is quoted on its own details.

Check the licence. Then design.

Taxi and private hire graphics are different from almost any other vehicle work, because the vehicle is licensed by a local council and the council’s conditions can affect what goes on the outside. Before you commission anything, read the current licensing policy and vehicle conditions from the authority that licenses your vehicle, and ask its licensing team if anything is unclear.

Councils set their own rules, and they can differ between neighbouring districts. Depending on where you are licensed, conditions may cover things such as door signs, required wording, the use of the word “taxi”, roof signs, livery colours, advertising, and whether signs must be fixed or removable. Some councils supply or specify particular signs or plates themselves. We cannot tell you which rules apply to your licence, so please check them with your council and send us any written requirements with your enquiry.

Built for the working van.

For a plumber, electrician, builder or landscaper, the van is often the first thing a new customer sees: parked on a driveway all day, waiting outside a merchant first thing in the morning, or lined up on a site next to other contractors. Trade van graphics have a simple job. They say who you are, what you do and how to reach you, clearly enough for someone walking past or sitting behind you in traffic.

That usually means fewer words than people expect. A list of twelve services in small lettering is hard to read from the pavement. Your business name, a short line that describes the trade (“Plumbing & heating”, “Domestic electrical”, “Landscaping & driveways”), a phone number and a web address do most of the work. Trade vans also come with practical constraints. Roof racks and ladders hide the top of the side panels. Racking, ply-lining and rear steps change how the van is loaded and where people stand. There are really three levels of coverage.

People often frame the decision as a wrap or just some stickers. In practice there are three broad approaches. Cut vinyl graphics put lettering, logos and contact details on the van’s own paint. A part wrap covers a defined section, such as the rear half or the lower panels, with printed or coloured film. A full wrap covers most or all of the painted body, either with a printed design or a single colour-change film.

Each is a sensible choice for some businesses and an expensive mistake for others. The deciding factors are what the van needs to say, how long you will keep it, whether you own it and how much of your budget belongs on the vehicle rather than elsewhere in your marketing.

Cut vinyl graphics: let the van’s colour do the work.

Lettering and logos on the existing paint are the classic form of van graphics. A clear company name, a short list of services, a phone number and a web address will tell people what they need to know. On a white van, a strong single colour is easy to read. A second colour, a panel infill or a printed logo adds character without the cost of covering whole panels.

Because the paint remains the background, design choices are mainly about hierarchy and spacing. Keep the name and number large enough to read from a distance and leave the panels uncluttered. This route also suits a business that expects details to change. A new phone number can be replaced as a single line of vinyl rather than a reprinted panel.

Our published supply-and-fit packages cover this approach. Basic starts from £149 + VAT, Standard from £210 + VAT and Pro from £455 + VAT, fitted within a 30-mile radius of our Norwich workshop and confirmed by a quote. See how much van graphics cost for what each includes.

Full wraps: the van becomes the advert.

A full wrap gives you the whole vehicle as a canvas. Photography, gradients, patterns and colours that run from bonnet to rear doors become possible, and the van can look nothing like the stock vehicle underneath. For a business where appearance is the product, such as a mobile café, a detailing service or an events company, that impact can be the point of the investment.

A wrap is also a bigger project. The design has to account for every door shut, handle, window, light and pressing, and the artwork must be planned so key elements are not lost across panel gaps. We produce mock-ups so you can see the design on your vehicle before anything is printed. Our printers produce prints roughly 1.5m wide by 50m long, so even large vehicles can be covered, and the film is chosen to suit the curves involved.

Wraps are quoted individually because the material, print and fitting time depend on the vehicle and the design. Ask for the quote to name the film and laminate so you know what you are paying for.

The middle ground: a part wrap.

A part wrap covers a planned section of the van, often the rear, the lower half or a band along each side. Combined with cut lettering on the remaining paint, it gives much of the visual impact of a full wrap with less material. It works best when the design treats the edge of the wrap as a deliberate line rather than an attempt to blend vinyl into paint.

Matching a vinyl colour exactly to a manufacturer’s paint colour is difficult, and the two can weather differently over time. Use the paint as a contrasting background, or choose a film colour that is clearly different. If your fleet includes vans in more than one paint colour, plan the part wrap so the design still looks consistent across them.

Repairs, removal and updates.

Think about what happens after the van leaves the workshop. If a panel is damaged, cut lettering on that panel can usually be replaced on its own. With a wrap, the affected section is reprinted, so keep the approved artwork and the film details together.

Vinyl graphics are semi-permanent: they can be replaced or removed. Removal time depends on the coverage, the age of the film and the condition of the paint. Covering more of the van means more to remove later. Paint under a wrap is shaded from sunlight, while uncovered paint is not, so a faint outline can sometimes show after removal on older vehicles. If you lease the van, read our guide to graphics on leased vans before choosing.

Three examples of how the brief changes the choice.

Illustrative example: a plumber with a new white panel van wants local customers to remember the name and number. Cut vinyl graphics with a printed logo do the job, keep the budget for other things and are straightforward to change if the van is replaced in a few years.

Illustrative example: a coffee van operator trades from events and the vehicle is the shopfront. A printed full wrap, designed around the serving hatch and the side that faces customers, does work that lettering cannot.

Illustrative example: a landscaping company runs several leased vans in different paint colours. A part wrap on the rear and lower panels with matching cut lettering keeps the fleet consistent, reduces the amount of film to remove at the end of each lease and still gives a strong presence on site.

Other finishes worth knowing about.

A colour-change wrap uses a single coloured or effect film rather than a print. It suits customers who want a different body colour, often with lettering added on top. We also offer liquid wrapping, a sprayed finish, including half liquid wrapping for partial coverage. If the vehicle is a company car rather than a van, our car graphics page covers the same choices on a smaller scale.

If you are undecided, ask for two options on the same vehicle: lettering or a part wrap, and a full wrap. Send the make, model, wheelbase, roof height and paint colour, with photographs of every side. Tell us how long you expect to keep the van and whether it is owned, leased or financed. We can then show you what each approach looks like and costs.

  • Photographs of both sides, the front and the rear.

Is a full wrap always better than graphics?

No. A wrap gives more visual impact, but clear lettering on the paint can be the better choice for a trade van that mainly needs to show a name and number. Choose around what the van needs to do.

Can I start with graphics and add a wrap later?

Yes. Graphics are semi-permanent, so lettering can be removed or reworked when you move to a wrap. Keep your artwork files so the new design can build on the old one.

An exact match is difficult, and paint and vinyl can age differently. A deliberate contrast usually looks better than a near match. We can show you film options at the design stage.

Vinyl covers the paint it sits on, but it is not a substitute for repairing damage. Paint condition affects both the fitting and the removal, so tell us about any repairs before work starts.

Cut lettering on the paint, especially if contact details sit on their own line. On a printed wrap it depends where the details are placed, so plan them as a replaceable element.

What to send us.

A few details help us quote accurately and design for the vehicle you actually have.

  • Make, model, year and roof height or wheelbase of each vehicle.
  • Photographs of both sides, the rear and the bonnet.
  • Your logo in a high-resolution or vector format, if you have one.
  • The wording: business name, services, phone, web and social details.
  • Whether the vehicle is owned, leased or financed.
  • For a fleet, the number of vehicles and when each is due.

Your questions. Answered.

Where is your workshop, and can I park there?

We are at Vulcan House, Vulcan Road North, Norwich, NR6 6AQ, on the airport side of the city. Journey time depends on your starting point and traffic, so use the directions link for the current route. Call 01603 407786 before you arrive to discuss parking, particularly for a larger vehicle.

Can I have a courtesy vehicle while my van is with you?

Courtesy vehicles are available while a van is off the road. Mention it when you book so we can check availability for your date.

Can you match graphics across a growing fleet?

Yes. Working from the approved artwork for your first vehicles, a new van can be lettered to match the existing ones, even if it is a different make or size. Tell us about vehicles due for replacement so the layout can be planned to suit them.

Can graphics go on a leased or electric vehicle?

Usually, yes. Vinyl is semi-permanent and can be removed later, but check your lease or finance agreement first and tell us the terms. Electric vans and cars take graphics in the same way as any other vehicle.

Do I need my own design?

No. Our in-house design department can create a layout from scratch, or work from your existing logo and brand colours.
